Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses vivid, real-time scenes for the story's most emotionally and dramatically charged moments—most notably the shooting in the synagogue, Barbara's chaotic push toward the exit, her immediate reunion with David outside, and the quiet concluding moment with the brass pin. These scenes ground the reader in the sensory details and immediate tension of the event. 

Simultaneously, the story makes strategic use of summary and exposition to provide necessary background (such as the setting of 1966 Detroit and Rabbi Adler's reputation) and to compress large spans of time following the trauma. By summarizing the aftermath—the newspaper coverage, the birth of Ruth, and the passing of decades—the author successfully bridges the gap between the inciting incident and the final reflective scene, illustrating the long-term psychological impact of the event on Barbara without bogging the narrative down in unnecessary details.
